title: The small village
hook: a small country where people hear the neighbor's dogs and roosters but are content at home (Tao Te Ching 80)

segments.voice: Yesterday, keep your half of the tally: after a quarrel, the sage holds his side of the agreement and asks nothing back. Your line was demand nothing. Which demand did you put down? Day one thousand one hundred forty-two.

A rooster, somewhere over the fence, before it's light. Then a dog two yards down answers it. A screen door. Somebody's radio. You can lie in bed and map the whole block by ear without ever seeing it. And still, the usual plan for the day is to get off that street: into the car, onto the highway, into the next thing. Chapter eighty of the Tao Te Ching stays on the street. It paints a whole country the size of a village, and it lets you hear the neighbors' animals through the walls.
screen: `A ROOSTER OVER THE FENCE.` → `A DOG ANSWERS.` → `A COUNTRY THE SIZE OF A VILLAGE.`

segments.voice: First, the size. Let the country be small, the chapter says, with few people. Give them tools that could do the work of many hands, and they leave them unused. Second, what they don't do. They take death seriously, so they don't wander far. They have boats and carriages, but no reason to ride in them. They have armor and weapons, but no occasion to lay them out. They even go back to knotting cords to keep their records. Third, what they do instead, and this is the heart of it. They find their food sweet. Their clothes fine. Their homes restful. Their customs a pleasure. Nothing in that list is new or rare. It's their own plate, their own coat, their own roof. Fourth, the ending. The next country is so close they can see it. They can hear its roosters crow and its dogs bark. And yet the people grow old and die without ever going back and forth. Readers take this differently. Some hear a dream of a simpler age, a ruler's picture of a quiet state. Some hear it as a picture of a heart: someone so at home that the far side of the fence doesn't pull at them. Nobody in the chapter is unfriendly. There's no wall, no quarrel, no fear of the neighbors. The barking is just a sound in the evening. Brought down to a weeknight, this looks like eating dinner and tasting it. Like walking your own block and finding something good on it.
screen: `A SMALL COUNTRY, FEW PEOPLE.` · `BOATS, BUT NO NEED TO RIDE.` · `SWEET FOOD, A RESTFUL HOME.` · `THEY HEAR THE DOGS NEXT DOOR.` · then, large: `CONTENT AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: enjoy your own street. Sit wherever you are and let the breath slow down. Now listen outward, past the room. What can you hear from right where you live? A car, a bird, a neighbor's door, a fridge humming, the wind. Don't go anywhere toward the sounds. Let them come to you. Then bring to mind one ordinary thing at home: a cup you like, a chair, a window. Let it be enough for a moment. The bell holds the time.
The small village. Chapter eighty: a small country where people find their food sweet and their homes restful, and hear the neighbors' dogs without needing to go. Today's word.
Your line: content at home. Today, walk to the end of your own street, or just to the window, and find one thing there worth noticing. Day one thousand one hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter eighty in more than one way: some read it as a picture of a simple, peaceful state, others as a picture of a contented life that doesn't need to chase what's beyond the fence.

fork.setup: you live in the small village. you can hear the roosters in the next country every morning. what does the chapter say the people do?
options: take a boat over to see it.
build a wall so they can't hear it.
grow old at home without going back and forth.
fork.reveal: they grow old and die without visiting. not out of fear: their food is sweet and their homes restful, so the far side doesn't pull at them.

original.note: Chinese: a small country, few people, the opening words of chapter eighty.

trapdoor: what you thought: the small village is about moving to the country.
what it means: contentment with your own food, clothes, home and customs, so there's no need to chase the place next door.
what a scholar hears: readers differ on whether the chapter is a political picture of a small state or a picture of an inner life; the text supports both.

notes: Chapter 80 is paraphrased throughout; the writer did not quote Legge because of uncertainty about his exact wording.
The teach calls chapter 80 'the next-to-last chapter', which holds in the received 81-chapter order; confirm the path uses that order.
The chapter speaks of returning to the use of knotted cords for records; paraphrased without further history.
Original 小國寡民 (xiǎo guó guǎ mín) rendered 'SHYOW gwaw GWAH meen'; confirm romanization and stress.
